extracted.intended_audience: Investigators and applicants seeking practical advice on applying for and managing NIH grants (postdocs, early-stage investigators, established PIs, grant administrators).
extracted.subtask_short: NIH grant application and funding advice
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, experience-based guidance on preparing NIH budgets and timelines, interacting with Program Officers (POs), interpreting application statuses and summary statements, eligibility for career awards (K99/K01), resubmission strategy, and award administration (JIT, NOA, start dates).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not include inflationary increases in NIH budgets
rubrics_metrics.description: NIH hasn’t allowed inflationary increases in grants for the last ~8 years; if you include them they will be cut.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead build in a cushion (suggested: a flat 10% across the years) because inflationary increases are almost certainly cut, leaving you to rebudget in future years if costs rise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build realistic budgetary cushions
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a modest, flat cushion across years rather than explicit inflation escalators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example recommended approach: a 10% flat cushion across years since explicit inflationary increases are likely to be removed during review/administrative processing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand IC processing delays and award timing
rubrics_metrics.description: ICs can be behind in processing awards (e.g., due to late appropriations or extraordinary events like COVID), so award actions may be delayed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect awards to be issued by September 30th of the fiscal year; start date is not an expiration date. If you must start spending earlier, get confirmation an award is planned within 90 days so your institution can set up pre-award spending.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Program Officers (POs) as an advisory resource
rubrics_metrics.description: POs can advise on paylines, whether to resubmit, and the reasonableness of start-up packages; they can help interpret summary statements and funding outlooks for their IC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Talk with your PO after you receive your summary statement for strategic advice. POs may know SRG tendencies and program priorities, and can sometimes provide candid assessments of competitiveness and funding likelihood.

rubrics_metrics.name: POs do not negotiate institutional start-up packages but may review them
rubrics_metrics.description: POs cannot negotiate your start-up package, but they see packages during the K99→R00 transition and can comment on whether a package is reasonable compared to norms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the PO thinks a package is unreasonable they can inform the Institution; POs often have experience comparing packages (including gender disparities) and can provide perspective to help you and your institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage other offers and pending grants in start-up negotiations
rubrics_metrics.description: If you lack external competing offers, pending R applications and mentor advocacy can provide leverage during start-up negotiations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek help from mentors, career development offices, CTSA resources, or faculty affairs to advise negotiation strategies; institutions have an interest in providing sufficient support to help new faculty succeed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeline expectations in proposals — provide a visual grid
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers expect an overall timeline (e.g., Year 1 do X, Year 2 do Y) rather than specific calendar dates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a visual grid broken into 4- or 6-month segments with columns as time segments and rows as Aims/sub-aims; shade boxes to show activity windows, parallel work, and feasibility across a 4–5 year project period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary statement release timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Summary statements for new R01 applications are prioritized and generally will be available well before council.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy indicates summary statements generally no later than 30 days before council. Release timing is in business days and can vary by SRO; contact SRO only if you have a time-sensitive need and have waited a reasonable time (eg, 4–5 weeks after study section).

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'Pending' statuses (administrative vs council)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Pending administrative review' usually means the application is being processed for award (often after JIT); 'Pending Council review' means someone needs to investigate the application status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume 'pending' guarantees an award; follow up with your PO or GMS if status stalls. If you must submit an A1 and haven't heard by institutional deadlines, submit (you can withdraw later if needed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding to JIT and award processing
rubrics_metrics.description: If JIT was requested, provide requested info promptly; administrative processing and NOA issuance require human sign-off and may be delayed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NOA issuance timing depends on staff availability and backlog; 'award prepared' is not instantaneous and may take days to weeks for final sign-off.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask your PO about changes to a pending project
rubrics_metrics.description: Minor changes to project focus (between closely related topics) are often acceptable, but substantive changes may be problematic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If changing the focal topic for an award in JIT (e.g., due to partner changes during COVID), ask your PO for approval; NIH has shown flexibility during the pandemic for reasonable changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplements and notifications practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions are not always notified if a supplement request is denied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you haven't heard about a supplement decision, email your PO—it's their job to know and to inform you if you ask.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing grants during investigator deployment
rubrics_metrics.description: Because NIH grants are awarded to institutions, if a PI is deployed the institution can designate another qualified PI to run the grant with NIH approval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short deployments (~6 months–1 year) are often manageable; discuss options with your institution and PO, and consider who could serve as interim PI if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: K99 eligibility tied to position that allows independent funding
rubrics_metrics.description: If your institutional position allows independent grant submission (PD/PI eligibility), you may be ineligible for K99.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if you don’t plan to submit independent grants during the K99, the position’s formal ability to apply makes you ineligible. Confirm with the PO before accepting a promotion/title that permits independent funding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effort allocation constraints when holding career awards
rubrics_metrics.description: Concurrent applications/awards depend on percent effort commitments (e.g., K01 at 75% may allow 25% effort on a separate R).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check award terms and discuss with your PO; if you lack uncommitted effort you may not be eligible to carry additional awards as PI until later years or transition to independent support.

rubrics_metrics.name: SEP reviews do not receive percentile rankings
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications reviewed by Special Emphasis Panels (SEPs) generally do not receive percentiles because SEPs do not meet each cycle required for percentile calculations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SEP-reviewed scores should still be considered for funding; RFA/SEP funding decisions also depend heavily on programmatic priorities and interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resubmission (A1) strategy should factor score, reviewer enthusiasm, and SRG fit
rubrics_metrics.description: High A0 scores (e.g., >40) that were not discussed may or may not be worth resubmitting; different reviewers or review panels can change outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult your PO and summary statement. If Significance scored well but reviewers lacked enthusiasm overall, consider reframing the scientific question or changing SRG/review panel to better match your work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary IC involvement and relinquishment process
rubrics_metrics.description: A secondary IC can consider your application only if the primary IC's PO relinquishes it and contacts the secondary IC; applicants do not control this process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secondary ICs rarely pick up fundable-but-above-payline applications; if you think a secondary IC fits, identify a PO there and discuss your science, but primary PO must initiate relinquishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budget size can affect funding decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Even fundable scores can be passed over if the requested budget is judged excessive for program priorities or IC constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you request an excess or large budget, be aware POs/ICs may opt not to fund despite an excellent percentile; discuss budget justification with your PO during JIT.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check institute-specific patterns and historical data
rubrics_metrics.description: Some ICs have idiosyncratic funding histories (e.g., few awards per year for certain mechanisms), affecting chances even with competitive scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use RePORT data and talk with your PO to understand typical funding practices in that IC and whether your application aligns with portfolio needs and historical award counts.
